title: Why Starbucks Wants Your Money First
summary: Customers loaded $15.2 billion onto Starbucks cards and rewards in one year, and $1.75 billion was still unspent at year end. Here's how prepaid money, breakage and a $7 billion Nestlé deal fund Starbucks.

hooks.hook: You load $25 onto the Starbucks app. You haven't ordered yet, but Starbucks already has your money.
In one year, $15.2 billion went onto Starbucks cards and rewards before anyone drank a thing.
Starbucks isn't a bank. But it holds your money like one.

sources: Starbucks FY2025 Form 10-K (fiscal year ended Sept 28, 2025), deferred revenue details (XBRL R76): stored value cards and loyalty program deferred revenue $1,751.7M at year end; additions $15,245.8M during FY2025; Nestlé up-front prepaid royalty $7,000.0M received Aug 26, 2018, recognized over an economic life of 40 years, $176.5M recognized per year; Nestlé balance $177.0M current + $5,600.0M noncurrent: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/829224/000082922425000114/R76.htm

Starbucks FY2025 10-K, accounting policies details (XBRL R48): stored value card and loyalty program breakage recognized $200.4M (company-operated stores) and $22.0M (licensed stores) in FY2025: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/829224/000082922425000114/R48.htm
Starbucks FY2025 10-K, income statement (XBRL R3): total revenues $37,184.4M: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/829224/000082922425000114/R3.htm
Starbucks FY2025 10-K, balance sheet (XBRL R7): deferred revenue $1,840.6M current + $5,772.6M long-term at Sept 28, 2025: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/829224/000082922425000114/R7.htm

Starbucks FY2025 10-K: "revenues from Starbucks Cards are recognized upon redemption and not when cash is loaded"; Starbucks Rewards defers revenue for Stars earned toward free product: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/829224/000082922425000114/sbux-20250928.htm

Stored value as "essentially an interest-free loan from the customer to the business" (Jack Raines, Sherwood News, Apr 23, 2024): https://sherwood.news/business/starbucks-could-use-a-cio-to-invest-the-usd2-2b-float-from-its-rewards
Our math: breakage $200.4M + $22.0M = $222.4M; / 365 days = about $609,000 a day.

scenes.narration: You load {$25|twenty-five dollars} onto the Starbucks app. You haven't ordered anything yet. But Starbucks already has your money.
Now multiply that by millions of people. In one year, more than {$15 billion|fifteen billion dollars} went onto Starbucks cards and rewards, before anyone drank a thing.
Starbucks isn't a bank. But it's holding a lot of money that isn't quite its own yet. Here's how that works.
Part one. Money first, coffee later.
Here's the order of things. You load the card. Starbucks gets the cash. Days or weeks later, you buy the drink. Only then does it count as a sale.
Starbucks' own annual report says it plainly. Revenue from its cards is recognized upon redemption, and not when cash is loaded.

data.quote: ...recognized upon redemption and *not when cash is loaded*

scenes.narration: In fiscal {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} {$15.2 billion|fifteen point two billion dollars} was added to those balances. Starbucks' total revenue that year was {$37.2 billion.|thirty-seven point two billion.}
And at the end of that year, {$1.75 billion|one point seven five billion dollars} was still sitting there, not yet spent.

data.label: on cards & rewards, not yet spent

scenes.narration: One writer put it simply. It's essentially an interest-free loan from the customer to the business.

data.quote: ...essentially an *interest-free loan* from the customer to the business

scenes.narration: If you like seeing the receipts behind everyday prices, subscribe. New ones every Tuesday and Friday.
Part two. The money nobody spends.
Some of that money never comes back for coffee. A gift card gets lost in a drawer. An app balance gets forgotten.
In fiscal {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} Starbucks booked about {$222 million|two hundred twenty-two million dollars} of what accountants call breakage. Money it expects nobody will ever spend.
That works out to more than {$600,000|six hundred thousand dollars} a day.
No coffee was made for it. No cup, no barista. It still becomes revenue.
Even the free drinks work this way. When you earn Stars, Starbucks sets aside part of what you paid, as a drink it owes you later.
Part three. The seven billion dollar head start.
Customers aren't the only ones who pay first. In {2018,|twenty eighteen,} Nestlé paid Starbucks {$7 billion|seven billion dollars} up front, for the right to sell Starbucks coffee in grocery stores.
Starbucks doesn't count it all at once. It spreads it over {40 years,|forty years,} about {$177 million|one hundred seventy-seven million dollars} a year.
At the end of fiscal {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} about {$5.8 billion|five point eight billion dollars} of it was still waiting to be counted.
Add it all up, and Starbucks' balance sheet shows {$7.6 billion|seven point six billion dollars} it has been paid, but hasn't counted as revenue yet.
Money first. Coffee later. Sometimes, coffee never.
So the next time an app asks you to load money before you order, remember who's giving the loan. It's you.
Starbucks sells coffee. But the cash shows up first. Next time: how casinos really make their money.
